title: A model-written fix beside each notebook finding, without touching the findings
request: The notebook copilot finds problems deterministically. Keep every finding exactly as it is; for each, ask a model for a fix in two sentences that cites the rule and the matching pitfall record, and show it under the finding. A finding never depends on the model. Test with the leaky bank-marketing notebook and a scripted client.
spec: The copilot reviews a notebook with a model for the explanations and code for the findings. Done when the leaky demo notebook gives the same findings as today, with a model-written fix per finding that cites the rule.
plan: Map the notebook copilot: detectors, how findings render, which records each cites.
While A3.3's review ran, write the core in files that review did not cover: copilot/fixes.py adds a fix key to a copy of each finding; the findings, severities, messages and proof are untouched.
After A3.3 was committed, add the gateway purpose notebook_review, the on-request route POST /api/projects/{id}/review/fixes, the CLI flag --fixes and a button on the Notebook page.
Check the page end to end with a scratch server whose model is scripted (nothing leaves the machine).

Run check-all; send A3.4 and the last A3.3 follow-ups to the reviewer together; fix over three rounds; verify the double-click guard in the real page with a slow scripted model that counts requests; commit.

decisions.decision: The fix is a separate key on a copy of the finding; nothing in a finding depends on a model.
decisions.why: The findings are the deterministic product; a model failure or a bad reply must not be able to change a severity, a message or the exit code.

decisions.decision: A fix is dropped unless every sentence passes the shared check and it cites one of the finding's rules and, where the finding has one, its pitfall or precedent record.
decisions.why: Citations are what code can check; a fix that cites nothing of its finding is advice without a source.

decisions.decision: The model sees each finding's title, message and suggestion and its records' text, with anything quoted from the code other than a plain name replaced, and two detectors redacted whole.
decisions.why: Findings quote the notebook's code (paths, selector strings, comparison values); the purpose says the model never sees the notebook's code or data.

decisions.decision: Fixes are requested by a person, one request at a time per project, keyed to their finding by detector, cell and line.
decisions.why: It is a model request with a cost; and a review can change between the GET and the POST, so matching by index can attach a fix to the wrong finding.

change: dclab_rnd/copilot/fixes.py (prompt building with redaction, chunks of eight findings, lenient parsing, the per-fix check); python -m dclab_rnd.copilot review NB --fixes; POST /api/projects/{id}/review/fixes with a per-project in-flight guard and fixes keyed by detector:cell:line; GET .../review says fixes_available; the Notebook page's companion shows each fix under the unchanged finding; cited.py follow-ups (number words, denial window, glued stops and dotted code names).

findings.defect: String literals from the notebook's code reached the prompt.
findings.scenario: A notebook with pd.read_csv on an absolute path holding a client folder name, a feature list with 'final <name>' and df['label <name>']: the marked names all appeared in the prompt, through the absolute_data_path message and the known_leakage_column and suspicious_column_name messages.
findings.cause: Finding messages were sent verbatim, and two detectors embed code literals in them.
findings.fix: Anything a finding quotes that is not a plain name becomes <code>; the absolute-path message is replaced by a fixed text.
findings.test: The data-limit test plants an absolute path and selector literals and finds none in the prompt.
findings.impact: A notebook's client folder names and column literals would be sent to the model provider, against the purpose's promise that the model never sees the notebook's code or data.
alternatives: Send a quoted name only when it fully matches an identifier pattern: tried first, but identifier-shaped literals such as a comparison value still passed (R1), so suspicious_column_name is now sent as <column>.

findings.defect: A fix could be attached to the wrong finding.
findings.scenario: Switching project during the request (up to 60 s) applied project A's fixes by index to project B's findings; a stage rerun between the GET and the POST shifted the indices, so a fix landed on a finding whose rule it never cited.
findings.cause: Fixes came back as a list matched by position, and the reply was applied to whatever review was on screen.
findings.fix: Fixes are keyed by detector:cell:line and matched on that key; the page ignores a reply for a review that is no longer the one on screen.
findings.impact: A fix written for project A's finding could be shown under project B's finding with A's rule chips, so a person would follow advice written for another problem.

findings.defect: The fixes request could fire twice.
findings.scenario: Any re-render during the request (apply fix, undo, a tab switch) rebuilt the button enabled, so a second paid request could start; the server had no guard.
findings.cause: The only guard was the button's disabled state.
findings.fix: A page flag survives re-renders, and the server answers 409 to a concurrent request for the same project.
findings.test: A route test for the 409; in the real page four rapid clicks made exactly one model request.
findings.impact: A re-render during the request could send a second paid model request, doubling the cost of asking for fixes.

findings.defect: Fixes that name dotted code were garbled while still labelled as cited.
findings.scenario: The fix '...ideally inside an imblearn.pipeline.Pipeline [DCLAB-R02]. The measured case shows why [PIT-003].' was stored as 'Pipeline. The measured case shows why.'
findings.cause: A3.3's new split at a stop glued to a capital split code names.
findings.fix: The dot of a code name does not end a sentence (see B4).
findings.impact: The fix for the oversampling finding names imblearn.pipeline.Pipeline; it was stored as the fragment 'Pipeline.' and still labelled as cited, so the advice the person reads is garbled.

findings.defect: The parser accepted booleans as finding numbers.
findings.scenario: {'finding': true} fixed finding 1 and false fixed finding 0.
findings.cause: isinstance(True, int) is true in Python.
findings.fix: Only a real integer is accepted; the status row states that a fix written for one finding passes on another sharing its rule and having no pitfall record.
findings.impact: A reply of {'finding': true} attached its fix to finding 1, which can be a different problem sharing a rule.
findings.open: A fix written for one finding still passes on another that shares its rule and has no pitfall record; citations are what is checked, not fit.

findings.defect: The request was unbounded and truncation failed silently.
findings.scenario: Ten findings made an 18.7k-character prompt; around 25 or more truncated the JSON at max_tokens 1500, the parser returned nothing, and the page said 'no fix passed the checks'; the CLI said nothing when a configured model failed.
findings.cause: One request for all findings and no message for that case.
findings.fix: Eight findings per request with global numbering; a failing chunk does not stop the others; the CLI prints a line when a model was asked and no fix passed.
findings.test: A test with a long review.
findings.impact: A notebook with many findings got no fixes and a misleading 'no fix passed the checks', and the CLI stayed silent when a configured model failed, so a person could not tell a model failure from a check.

findings.defect: The shared check let some number words through unchecked.
findings.scenario: Kept against sources with no matching number: 'improved by one percent', 'a one-point gain', 'Hundreds of rows', 'Dozens of columns'; 'twenty-one rows' was kept against 20.
findings.cause: 'one' was always exempt, plurals were not number words, and compounds were read as their first word.
findings.fix: 'one' is a number before percent, point, fold and similar; compounds are read whole; plural multipliers must be words of a cited source.
findings.impact: 'improved by one percent' or 'Hundreds of rows' was kept with no matching number in the source, so invented magnitudes passed as checked.

findings.defect: A count word lost its unit.
findings.scenario: 'It has ten percent' was kept against a source saying '10 candidates'; '10 percent' in digits was correctly dropped.
findings.fix: A following percent, thousand or million is attached to the count word.
findings.impact: 'ten percent' passed against a source saying '10 candidates', changing what the number means.

findings.defect: The four-word denial window reopened double negatives.
findings.scenario: Kept: 'I do not doubt it is production-ready', 'We cannot deny it is production-ready', 'It is not wrong to call it production-ready', 'It does not fail to be production-ready'.
findings.fix: The window may not contain doubt, deny, wrong, fail, unlike, hard or unreasonable.
findings.impact: 'We cannot deny it is production-ready' would be shown as an explanation or fix, the forbidden claim in a double negative.

findings.defect: Splitting at a stop plus a capital mangled dotted code names.
findings.scenario: 'Wrap it in pd.DataFrame first [A].' was kept as 'DataFrame first.'; 'Use sklearn.pipeline.Pipeline to fit the scaler [A].' as 'Pipeline to fit the scaler.'
findings.cause: The glued-stop rule did not know code names.
findings.fix: A stop between letters inside a dotted name, or after a known module prefix, does not split.
findings.impact: Explanations and fixes naming pd.DataFrame or sklearn.pipeline.Pipeline were cut to fragments, so the code advice made no sense.
alternatives: Protect any token that contains a dot or is shorter than about four characters: tried in the next round and replaced in R3, because short tokens let 'It is OK.It scored ...' merge an uncited claim; a list of module prefixes is protected instead.

findings.defect: Identifier-shaped literals from the code still reached the prompt (second round).
findings.scenario: df[df['status'] == 'closed_<marker>'] produced 'Check when `closed_<marker>` is created' and the marker, a cell value, was in the prompt; a backtick inside a path literal defeated the plain-name rule.
findings.cause: suspicious_column_name quotes any string in a subscript, including comparison values, and plain() kept any backticked name.
findings.fix: suspicious_column_name is sent as <column>; the absolute-path message is a fixed text.
findings.test: The data-limit test plants an underscore name, a comparison value and a backtick path.
findings.impact: A comparison value from the notebook's code, which is a cell value, would be sent to the model provider.

findings.defect: 'one-' before any hyphen was read as the number 1.
findings.scenario: 'Fit the one-hot encoder', 'one-vs-rest', 'one-class', 'one-time cost' and 'at one point' were dropped when the source had no 1; the copilot flags OneHotEncoder, so fixes often say one-hot.
findings.cause: The B1 fix read 'one' before any hyphen.
findings.fix: 'one' is a number only before point, percent, fold, times, in and similar.
findings.impact: Fixes saying 'one-hot encode inside the fold', common advice because the copilot flags OneHotEncoder, were dropped as invented numbers, so findings lost their fix.
findings.open: 'A one-percent sample' is dropped against a source that writes '1 percent', a fail-closed loss.

findings.defect: Single-word module names still split, and some uncited prefixes still merged.
findings.scenario: 'Use imblearn.Pipeline so the sampler runs in the fold [A]' was kept as 'Pipeline so the sampler runs in the fold.'; 'It is OK.It scored 0.9248 [A].' merged because short tokens were protected.
findings.cause: Protection by token length instead of by known module prefixes.
findings.fix: Only a list of module prefixes (np, pd, sklearn, imblearn, torch and others) is protected before a capital; every other stop plus capital splits.
findings.impact: 'Use imblearn.Pipeline so the sampler runs in the fold' was kept as a fragment, while 'It is OK.It scored 0.9248' merged an uncited claim.

findings.defect: A module name wrapped in backticks, quotes or parentheses still split (third round).
findings.scenario: 'Convert it with `pd.DataFrame` first [A].' was kept as 'DataFrame` first.'; '(sklearn.Pipeline)' and '"pd.DataFrame"' the same; aliases such as xgb, lgb, pathlib and polars were missing.
findings.cause: The token kept its opening punctuation, so the prefix was not found in the list.
findings.fix: Leading punctuation is stripped before the lookup, and the module list gained the missing aliases.
findings.test: Tests for the three wrapped forms.
findings.impact: A model that writes code names in backticks, as the findings' own suggestions do, would have its fixes garbled.
findings.open: A glued stop followed by a lowercase word still merges; it cannot be told apart from a dotted name such as pandas.read_csv.

measurements.name: the leaky bank-marketing notebook with a scripted model
measurements.gate: The same findings as before the change, and a fix per finding that cites its rule (the package's Done-when).
measurements.result: All 10 findings identical to before; each gets a fix citing its rule and its pitfall or precedent record (for example DCLAB-R02 and PIT-003 for the oversampling finding).
measurements.next: A fix's quality (is the advice right) is not measured; the model path is tested with a scripted model only.
measurements.against_gate: All 10 findings are identical to before, the first half of the gate; each gets a fix citing its rule and its pitfall or precedent record, the second half: the gate is met.
limits: One notebook, the leaky bank-marketing demo, whose findings the copilot already knew.
The model is scripted and its replies were written to pass, so the run shows the plumbing and the checks, not what a real model writes.
Whether a fix is good advice is not measured; only its citations and numbers are checked.
A fix written for one finding can pass on another that shares its rule and has no pitfall record.

outcome: Done: findings unchanged, a checked and cited fix beside each when a person asks, from the CLI or the Notebook page, with the notebook's code and data kept out of the prompt. Open: only the project's own exported notebook is reviewed in the product; notebook_assist is untouched; a fix's quality beyond the checks is not measured. The gate passed with 508 tests; fourteen review findings over three rounds fixed.
lessons: Messages written for humans quote the input; before sending findings to a model, list every detector that embeds code and redact by shape, then plant each shape in a test.
Match asynchronous results to stable keys, never to list positions on a screen that can change.
Each fix to a text splitter opens a new edge (code names, wrapped names, short tokens); keep the reviewer's exact probes as tests.
risks: Finding messages quoting the notebook's code literals (paths, selectors, comparison values) into the prompt.
A model reply changing a finding's severity, message or the exit code.
Fixes matched to findings by list position when the review can change between the GET and the POST.
Paid requests fired twice from the page.
A long review overrunning the reply's token limit and failing silently.
